upper_bound.quote: * (ii) there is $c>0$ such that $V \subseteq \{0, c\}$ with both values attainable.
upper_bound.witness: NON-SEQUITUR. What §3 establishes is only: V contains at most one POSITIVE number (the rational/irrational-ratio argument compares two positive values c_1 > c_2 > 0). The text nowhere proves g(x) = f(x) - x >= 0 for all x (the standard argument, that f^n(t) = t + n d(t) must stay positive so d(t) >= 0, is absent; §1 only gives g(x) > -x). Hence from 'at most one positive value' one cannot conclude V ⊆ {0} or V ⊆ {0,c}: a priori V could contain negative values, or one positive value together with negative values, and then the parenthetical 'every x>0 belongs to S_0 ∪ S_c' fails. All later steps (the level-set inequalities (10)-(12), Lemma 1's use of 'b = g(z) ∈ {0,c}', and the covering argument) presuppose this unjustified dichotomy.
upper_bound.load_bearing: The whole necessity argument (§4-§7) is a case analysis over the alleged two-element value set {0, c}; if negative values of g are not excluded, neither the exclusion of mixed fixed/non-fixed points nor the conclusion g ≡ c is established for all x.

parsed.notes: Identity f(f(x))=2f(x)-x and the AP relation g(x+g(x))=g(x) are correctly derived; verification via QM-AM and AM-GM covers both inequalities for all c>=0. The necessity argument omits proving g >= 0, so 'at most one positive value' does not yield V ⊆ {0,c}, on which §4-§7 depend.
